item.title: Rational quantum spectral filtering by repeat-until-success protocol
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Real rational functions R(x) bounded by [0,1] with no poles on [−1,1] can be synthesized exactly on quantum walks with controller memory dimension d satisfying rational degree r≤d2, bypassing polynomial approximation.

Grade 0.438 · 3.0σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum singular value transformation and beyond: exponential improvements for…” · Maksim A. Gavreev, Aleksey K. Fedorov, Evgeniy O. Kiktenko

Figure

RUS protocol framework showing the circuit architecture, first-hitting transition graph, and resulting rational spectral filtering response R(x)=P(x)/Q(x) across eigenvalue x.

Asks

Can a finite-memory repeat-until-success architecture with mid-circuit measurements implement rational spectral effects exactly without polynomial approximation?

But

Requires uniform termination and phase-inversion symmetry; spectrum of Hermitian operator X must lie in [−1,1]; bounds derived under fresh-copy, terminal-postselection restarting model.

Tools

repeat-until-success (RUS) protocol · qubitized quantum walk · discrete Lyapunov equation · Fejér–Riesz spectral factorization · mid-circuit flag measurement

Abstract

We introduce a finite-memory repeat-until-success (RUS) framework for implementing rational spectral filters on a quantum computer, extending spectral filtering beyond the polynomial transformations implemented by quantum signal processing (QSP) and quantum singular value transformation (QSVT). Our approach interleaves queries to a block encoding of a Hermitian operator X, whose spectrum lies in [-1,1], and mid-circuit measurements that either accept, reject, or continue the computation without resetting the quantum state. Although the protocol may run for arbitrarily many rounds, its terminal statistics are determined by a finite-dimensional Lyapunov equation. Under uniform termination and phase-inversion symmetry, we characterize exactly the spectral filters R(X) realizable upon acceptance: R can be any real rational function with no poles on [-1,1] and values in [0,1]. We provide a constructive compiler for any admissible R, with bounds on memory and expected query cost, and characterize the accepted quantum operation through a spectral coherence kernel. Applications to regularized resolvents and Lorentzian spectroscopy yield exact low-degree realizations and query-cost advantages over the fixed-depth QSVT polynomial-postselection baseline considered here, with all repetitions and independent restarts after rejection included in the cost.

item.title: The energetic cost of loading classical data in quantum computers
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Querying a 12-qubit address bucket-brigade QRAM on superconducting hardware consumes 3.51×10−4J of dynamic energy at query fidelity 0.969. Average dynamic power is 4.38W with a peak of 64.4W.

Grade 0.428 · 2.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum algorithms with provable speedup, query and gate complexity bounds” · Joao F. Doriguello, Alessandro Luongo, Harshit Verma

Asks

What is the dynamic energetic cost and power consumption of a QRAM query on superconducting processors when constrained by query fidelity?

But

Theoretical simulation using superconducting microwave drive models, accounting for thermal photons and gate errors without active error correction.

Tools

metric-noise-resource framework · bucket-brigade QRAM architecture · linear-depth multiplexer QRAM · superconducting gate decomposition · multi-stage dilution refrigerator attenuation model

Abstract

Quantum algorithms for machine learning, chemistry, and cryptanalysis often assume coherent access to classical data at negligible physical cost. We instead treat data loading as a hardware process and quantify the dynamic energetic cost of a quantum random access memory (QRAM) query on a superconducting processor. Using the metric-noise-resource framework, we relate query fidelity and power to gate duration, relative two-qubit drive strength, and the distribution of attenuation across a multi-stage refrigerator, while accounting for thermal photons and gate errors. We analyze the linear-depth multiplexer and the noise-resilient bucket-brigade architectures, adapting the latter to a native superconducting gate set and refining its fidelity analysis using the fully decomposed gate schedule. For a representative bucket-brigade QRAM query with a 12-qubit address register we obtain a query fidelity of 0.969. The query consumes 3.51×10⁻⁴ J of dynamic energy, corresponding to an average dynamic power of 4.38 W and a peak of 64.4 W. Our optimization shows that, at fixed target fidelity, the operating point and attenuation profile can change the average power by a factor of two or more.

item.title: Classical phase unwrapping enables large-time-step unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization
item.description:
Pay dirt new method — Classical unwrapping post-processing recovers aliased unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization energies with errors ≤1.1×10−7 Ha noiseless, and median errors within chemical accuracy under Gaussian noise σ=10−4 using small Krylov dimensions M=20--65.

Grade 0.399 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Tushar Kumar Jain, Rahul Maitra, Nicholas J. Mayhall

Figure

Median energy error under Gaussian noise σ=10−4 versus time step τ for ground and first excited states across six molecules. Plain UQKSD fails once aliasing begins, whereas CURE-QKSD maintains chemical accuracy deep into the aliased regime.

Asks

Can energy aliasing from large time steps in unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization be robustly corrected via classical post-processing to avoid numerical ill-conditioning?

Before

Uncorrected principal-branch UQKSD at these aliased time steps gave errors of 0.7--115 Ha, or required small unaliased time steps yielding ill-conditioned overlap matrices.

But

Target energies must fall within classical window; phantom peaks from two colliding states are not excluded; no formal error bounds.

Tools

unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (UQKSD) · CURE-QKSD phase unwrapping · generalized eigenvalue problem · classical energy windows (CCSD / Hartree-Fock)

Abstract

For computing molecular energies on early fault-tolerant hardware, unitary quantum Krylov subspace diagonalization (UQKSD) avoids both the deep circuits of quantum phase estimation and the Pauli-term sampling of variational methods by extracting the energies from a projected real-time propagator. At a small time step τ, nearly linearly dependent Krylov vectors make the overlap matrix ill-conditioned. Our tests at fixed total evolution time show that additional Krylov vectors then add no accuracy, while the thresholded energy becomes increasingly sensitive to the choice of cutoff. A larger time step improves the conditioning and reduces the Krylov dimension M needed for a target accuracy, but the energies are then known only modulo 2π/τ. We present Classical Unwrapping for Resolving Eigenvalues (CURE-QKSD), a classical post-processing method that leaves the UQKSD circuits and generalized eigenvalue problem unchanged and recovers the missing multiples of 2π/τ from phase-consistency landscapes of one or, when needed, two UQKSD runs. In noiseless tests on six molecules with 12--20 qubits, all 28 targeted energies are recovered in their aliased regimes with final errors of at most 1.1×10⁻⁷~Ha. Under Gaussian noise with σ=10⁻⁴, the median error of the ground or first excited state reaches chemical accuracy at large aliased time steps with M=20--65, whereas uncorrected principal-branch energies are off by 0.7--115~Ha. CURE-QKSD therefore makes aliased time steps usable for UQKSD calculations with smaller, better-conditioned Krylov bases.

item.title: Cross-Platform Benchmarking of GHZ-State Generation in Quantum Processors via Cloud Services
item.description:
Pay dirt new result — Large superconducting quantum processors (107 to 156 qubits) support GHZ states passing genuine multipartite entanglement non-exclusion criteria on at most N∗=27 and N∗=24 qubits (<23% of register), whereas a 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes on its full register (N∗=12). Under a strict GME certification rule, only four of nine commercial processors succeed at any tested size.

Grade 0.397 · 2.4σ above the day's baseline · matched “Quantum supremacy using a programmable superconducting processor” · Sergio Hernández, Unai Aseguinolaza, David Aguirre, Marta Gili, Joseba Hernández, Guillermo Valverde, Uxue Ballarin Manso, Uxue Auzmendi, Iker Pastor, Pablo García Bringas, Ane Blázquez García, Rubén Peña, Mikel Sanz

Figure

Comparison of largest passing GHZ size N∗ against total physical qubits Ntot, alongside register utilization ratios and per-qubit GHZ error rates across nine processors.

Asks

How do commercial cloud-accessible quantum computing platforms across different hardware modalities compare when preparing genuine multipartite entangled GHZ states under standard end-user compilation?

But

Default provider compilations without error mitigation; stabilizer sample size set by ε=δ=0.10; evaluations limited to single runs or sparse binary-searched register sizes.

Tools

QuSquare benchmark suite · Direct Fidelity Estimation (DFE) · remote cloud-access APIs (Amazon Braket, Qiskit Runtime) · superconducting and trapped-ion QPUs

Code. https://github.com/NQUIRE-Center/Cross-Platform-Benchmarking/tree/main/GHZ-State_Generation

Abstract

Quantum computing has rapidly evolved into a diverse ecosystem of hardware platforms that differ in their underlying technologies and operational characteristics. Consequently, benchmarking has become essential for identifying the strengths of quantum processors, comparing their performance, and enabling informed decisions when selecting the most appropriate quantum computing platform for specific applications. In this work, we benchmark nine commercially accessible quantum processors from five vendors, spanning superconducting and trapped-ion technologies, using the multipartite entanglement benchmark from the QuSquare suite. All experiments were performed through remote cloud-access services, with the default compilation of each provider and without error mitigation, reflecting the performance experienced by end users. The benchmark estimates the fidelity of Greenberger--Horne--Zeilinger (GHZ) states by direct fidelity estimation and searches for the largest GHZ state whose fidelity is compatible, within the statistical error, with the genuine multipartite entanglement (GME) threshold F=1/2. Our results reveal a substantial gap between the total number of physical qubits available on a processor and the size of the largest GHZ state passing the benchmark: the best superconducting processors reach N^*=27 and N^*=24 qubits, less than a quarter of their registers, whereas the 12-qubit trapped-ion processor passes with its full register. We further show that median calibration data are poor predictors of the benchmark outcome, and that the reported sizes depend strongly on the statistical decision rule: requiring certified GME reduces the number of devices that succeed at any tested size from nine to four. These results provide a baseline for future cross-platform benchmarking of quantum processors.

item.title: Early State Exclusion for 5×5 Jacobi Matrices
item.description:
Pay dirt theory — A 5×5 persymmetric Jacobi matrix with centered spectrum {c−x,c−y,c,c+y,c+x} realizing perfect state transfer lacks early state exclusion if and only if x is an integer multiple of y. Any prescribed even number 2k of early state exclusions can be generated by setting positive eigenvalues y=2k+1 and x=2k+2.

Grade 0.382 · 2.1σ above the day's baseline · matched “quantum linear algebra, block encodings and singular value transformation” · Jasmin G. Enriquez, Anastasiia Minenkova

Figure

State overlap |⟨e−iJt𝐞0,𝐞0⟩| versus time t showing multiple zeros (early state exclusions) prior to perfect state transfer at t=π when x is not an integer multiple of y.

Asks

Can early state exclusion occur in a 1D quantum spin chain of 5 qubits that realizes perfect state transfer?

Before

Early state exclusion was proven impossible for 3 qubits and constructed for all even numbers of qubits, but remained open for all odd numbers n>4.

But

Applies strictly to 5×5 Jacobi matrices with centered or symmetric spectra and nearest-neighbor interactions; odd qubit counts n≥7 remain unproven.

Tools

Sylvester formula · Jacobi matrix reconstruction · persymmetric matrix eigentheory · Intermediate Value Theorem

Abstract

In this paper, we present a problem that arose from quantum computing, when the quantum state to be transferred completely vanishes before the first occurrence of the perfect state transfer. It was posed as an open problem for 1D quantum chains with n of qubits, where n>4 is an odd number. We present the solution for n=5. The proofs are accessible to students who studied trigonometry and calculus. As for the set-up the knowledge of eigentheory and inner products from linear algebra is needed.

item.title: Normalizing Flows for Classical Simulation of Quantum Circuits in Phase Space
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Classical fidelity of continuous normalizing flows over (S2)N phase space reaches F≈0.96 at N=64 qubits for 1D cluster states and 0.985 at gate 40 for a 10-qubit TFIM VQE circuit.

Grade 0.367 · 1.9σ above the day's baseline · matched “Hamiltonian Simulation by Qubitization” · Edward Jiang, Timothy Heightman, Marcin Płodzień

Figure

Classical fidelity between predicted and exact distributions plotted against total qubits N for 1D cluster and GHZ state preparation, comparing continuous normalizing flows against IC-POVM and NQS baselines.

Asks

Can quantum circuits be simulated classically by parameterizing unitary gates as normalizing flows between phase-space probability distributions on (S2)N?

Before

For 1D cluster states at N=60, IC-POVM reached 0.91 and NQS reached 0.84; for 10-qubit TFIM VQE, transformer IC-POVM reached 0.965.

But

Training cost scales as 𝒪(K2) for K gates because evaluating prior states requires inverting all previous flows; entangling-gate flows are state-dependent and cannot be reused for different input states.

Tools

Husimi Q function phase-space representation · continuous normalizing flows on (S²)^N · multi-layer perceptrons · KL divergence Monte Carlo minimization

Abstract

We present a novel framework to learn a representation of quantum circuits based on the phase space formulation of many-body systems. Given that N-qubit states can be represented as probability distributions on a smooth 2N-dimensional manifold, we show how unitary gates can be parameterized as normalizing flows between these distributions, opening a new avenue for quantum circuit simulation using generative models. We evaluate our method on three common families of quantum circuits, and show that its accuracy exceeds that of current state-of-the-art neural network methods for large system sizes.

item.title: Secure Information Flow in Quantum Programs
item.description:
Worth a look new method — Formulated noninterference 𝖭𝖨 and simulation-based 𝖲𝖨𝖬 security for quantum programs, proved 𝖭𝖨⇔𝖲𝖨𝖬⇔𝖲𝖨𝖬𝖰, and developed self-conjugation to verify them via quantum Hoare logic.

Grade 0.361 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “dequantization and classical algorithms that match quantum claims” · Zhicheng Zhang, Mingsheng Ying, Lirong Xia

Figure

Information flow through circuit Q and its reverse Q†. Red lines mark secret data propagation, comparing insecure flow that leaks into low variables against secure flow confined to high and environmental variables.

Asks

How do we formally define and verify information-flow security for quantum programs?

But

Loop-free quantum programs with finite-dimensional variable types (or fixed-bound unrolled loops).

Tools

quantum Hoare logic · self-conjugation · deferred measurement principle · program dilation

Abstract

Information-flow security aims to prevent the leakage of confidential information through program execution. This problem becomes fundamentally subtler for quantum programs, because their states may involve superposition and entanglement, and their executions may involve intricate interactions between classical and quantum variables. This paper develops semantic foundations and verification methods for secure information flow in quantum programs. We formulate two notions of information-flow security. The first is a noninterference-based definition that naturally generalizes its classical counterpart. The second is a simulation-based definition that explicitly models an attacker, providing a clear operational interpretation of security. We prove that these two notions are equivalent. To verify the information-flow security of quantum programs, we develop a proof framework based on quantum Hoare logic. A key challenge is that the standard self-composition technique, which expresses information-flow security in Hoare logic by composing a program with a renamed copy of itself, fails in the quantum setting due to an obstruction analogous to the no-cloning theorem. To overcome this challenge, we introduce self-conjugation, a novel technique that leverages the deferred measurement principle and properties of unitary operations. We demonstrate our framework on examples drawn from the quantum one-time pad, quantum error correction, and anonymous entanglement generation.

item.title: A Hardware-Trained Generative Quantum Eigensolver for Sample-Based Quantum Diagonalization of Organotin Hydroxides up to 70 Qubits
item.description:
Worth a look new result — GQE transformer policy trained directly on a 70-qubit processor generates state-preparation circuits that recover energies within 15 mHa of DMRG across 27 of 28 test runs (median 4.5 mHa). Circuits at 56–70 qubits require 34–72 times fewer two-qubit gates than transpiled LUCJ ansätze.

Grade 0.358 · 1.8σ above the day's baseline · matched “Toward the first quantum simulation with quantum speedup” · Kunal Kumar, Kimberlee Keithley, Toshiya Iwamori, Shu Kanno, Ikko Hamamura, Takao Kobayashi, Akira Koseki, Qi Gao, Naoki Yamamoto, Hiroshi Horii, Yuri Kobayashi, Borja Peropadre, Kouhei Nakaji, Toru Imai, Takayuki Osogami

Figure

Excitation distribution (HF, single, double, triple, quadruple, higher) plotted across 10 sampled circuits for eleven organotin molecules from 32 to 70 qubits, showing physical shot spread across excitation manifolds without collapsing to Hartree–Fock.

Asks

Can generative quantum eigensolver policies be trained directly with quantum hardware feedback at active spaces up to 70 qubits beyond exact classical simulation?

But

Single training run per lineage. Evaluated on 10 sampled circuits per molecule with up to 100,000 shots per circuit; subspace recovery capped at 20,000 strings.

Tools

generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) · sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD) · IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe · GRPO/GSPO policy-gradient training

Abstract

Quantum hardware can provide feedback for training circuit generators beyond the reach of exact classical simulation. We train generative quantum eigensolver (GQE) policies, transformers conditioned on molecular descriptors, to generate the state-preparation circuits for sample-based quantum diagonalization (SQD). Training runs first on a noiseless simulator and then with the IBM Heron processor ibm_kobe inside the loop, at 46 and 70 qubits (1.2 ×10⁸ shots for the four main training runs). A classical CCSD(T) reference energy of the training molecules enters only an admission gate and two auxiliary reward terms. During hardware training, a reward penalty prevents collapse to circuits that sample only the Hartree-Fock determinant. Policies trained on transition-metal complexes are applied without retraining to Sn(OH)₃-Me and its hydrates, minimal models of organotin photoresists for extreme-ultraviolet lithography, from 32 to 70 qubits. After one round of hardware sampling, followed by classical ranking and recovery of the cached counts with the molecular Hamiltonian and no further QPU calls, 27 of 28 runs at 46-70 qubits are within 15 mHa of the density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) reference (median 4.5 mHa), and in all eight runs with an untrained control the trained policy is more accurate. At 56-70 qubits the selected circuits use 34-72 times fewer two-qubit gates than the local unitary cluster Jastrow (LUCJ) circuit transpiled for the same device. These results demonstrate that circuit generators can be trained with quantum hardware at 70 qubits.
